h1: The 8 Best Compost Tumblers Under $200 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 compost tumblers under $200 scored on capacity, chamber design, frame strength and ease of turning, from 22 to 53 gallons.
summary: The Maygrove 53 gallon is the tumbler to buy if you want the most space and a steel frame: dual chambers, sliding doors and 360 degree rotation. The Cozurra 45 gallon is the close second. The VIVOSUN and Werph 43 gallon units are the budget workhorses, FCMP's 37 gallon steel drum is the odd-shape alternative, and the FCMP IM2000 at 22 gallons is the one for a small garden.
intro: The usual compost-tumbler mistake is buying by drum size and ignoring the frame. A full drum is heavy, and every turn lifts that weight on the bearings and the legs. Cheap stands wobble, flex and, in the worst cases, crack where the axle meets the frame. The gallon number on the box says nothing about whether the thing will still spin in its third summer.

So this ranking leans on the structure as much as the capacity. We compared eight tumblers under $200 on drum size, whether the drum has two chambers so one batch can cure while the other fills, the frame material, the door design and how easily you can turn a full load. Where a listing states little, we say so rather than fill the gap.

products.name: Maygrove Outdoor Compost Bin 53 Gallon, Dual Chamber Large Compost Tumbler
products.verdict: The biggest drum here, with two chambers, sliding doors and a solid steel frame.
products.description:
Maygrove's 53 gallon tumbler is the largest in the ranking, with dual chambers, sliding doors, 360 degree rotation and a solid steel frame. Two chambers are the feature that changes how you compost: one side matures while you fill the other, so you never have to stop adding scraps.

It wins because it pairs the biggest capacity with the sturdiest build listed. Against the Cozurra at 45 gallons, you get more room and a stated steel frame; against the 43 gallon budget units, the frame is the upgrade that matters over years. Sliding doors also keep soil and scraps from spilling the way hinged lids sometimes do.

Buy it for a family that generates steady kitchen and yard waste. It sits in the $100 to $200 bracket, and a 53 gallon drum gets heavy when full, so do not overload it.
cons: Heavy when the drum is full
products.idealFor: Households with steady kitchen and garden waste.
products.skipIf: You have a small patio or little waste to compost.

products.name: Cozurra 45 Gallon Large Compost Tumbler Outdoor, Dual Chamber Compost Bin
products.verdict: A 45 gallon dual-chamber tumbler that sits between the budget units and the Maygrove.
products.description:
Cozurra offers 45 gallons with a dual-chamber design, in the $100 to $200 bracket alongside the Maygrove. The dual chambers are the real selling point, since they let you run two stages of composting at the same time.

It ranks second because the Maygrove adds eight gallons and a stated steel frame. The listing is short on construction detail, so the structure is an unknown here. The 43 gallon units below cost less for nearly the same capacity, so the Cozurra only makes sense if you prefer its design or find it in stock at a good price.

A fit for a mid-size household with a medium garden. The caveat is the thin spec sheet: check the frame, door latch and rotation details on the listing before ordering.
products.idealFor: Mid-size households with a medium garden.
products.skipIf: You want a stated steel frame or lower price.

products.name: VIVOSUN Outdoor Tumbling Composter Dual Rotating Batch Compost Bin, 43 Gallon
products.verdict: A 43 gallon dual rotating batch bin with a black door, in the $50 to $100 range.
products.description:
VIVOSUN's tumbler holds 43 gallons in a dual rotating batch design with a black door, and it sits in the $50 to $100 bracket. Batch means you fill one side, stop adding to it and let it finish while you load the second.

It ranks third because it delivers dual-chamber composting at a lower price than Cozurra or Maygrove. Against the Werph, the two share the same capacity and the same price tier, so the choice comes down to the brand and the details in the listing. The cost of the saving is fewer stated features than the Maygrove, which spells out its frame.

A strong pick for a first compost setup. The listing is short on construction detail, so check frame and door information before you order.
pros: Dual batch design at low price
products.idealFor: First-time composters who want two chambers on a budget.
products.skipIf: You need a stated steel frame.

products.name: Werph 43 Gal Dual Chamber Compost Bin Tumbler for Backyard Garden, Black
products.verdict: A black 43 gallon dual-chamber tumbler in the same price tier as VIVOSUN.
products.description:
Werph sells a 43 gallon dual-chamber tumbler in black for the $50 to $100 range. The listing gives few other specs, so the dual chamber and capacity are what you can rely on.

It ranks fourth because VIVOSUN offers the same capacity and chamber layout with a clearer batch-style description. The two are close enough that either is fine; the difference is how much detail each seller provides. Against the bundles below, Werph does not add gardening gloves, but it is a cleaner single-product listing.

A reasonable pick for a small to medium garden. The caveat is the thin information: look for the frame material and the door seal in the photos before you commit.
pros: Two chambers at a low price
products.idealFor: Small to medium gardens on a tight budget.
products.skipIf: You want construction details before buying.

products.name: FCMP Outdoor Heavy Duty 37 Gallon 8 Sided Steel Composter, Black
products.verdict: An eight-sided steel drum at 37 gallons, built to be heavy duty.
products.description:
FCMP's composter is an eight-sided steel drum of 37 gallons, sold in the $50 to $100 bracket. An eight-sided shape gives the contents more to tumble against than a smooth round barrel, which helps mix scraps and browns.

It ranks fifth because the capacity is the smallest of the full-size units and the listing does not mention dual chambers. Against the 43 gallon units above, you give up space and the continuous-batch routine. In return you get a steel drum, which is a different material from the plastic barrels on most tumblers here.

Choose it for a household that wants a robust single drum. The caveat is that with only one chamber you must stop adding scraps while the batch cures.
products.idealFor: Households wanting a sturdy single steel drum.
products.skipIf: You want to add scraps continuously.

products.name: Compost Tumbler Bin Composter Dual Chamber 43 Gallon (Bundled with Pearson's Gardening Gloves)
products.verdict: A dual-chamber 43 gallon tumbler that includes a pair of Pearson's gardening gloves.
products.description:
This is a 43 gallon dual-chamber tumbler sold as a bundle with Pearson's gardening gloves, in the $50 to $100 bracket. The gloves are a small extra, and useful, since handling compost is dirty work.

It ranks sixth because the tumbler itself has the same headline specs as the VIVOSUN and Werph, with less information on the maker. The bundle is the only difference, and gloves are not a reason to pick a tumbler over a better-documented one. It is a fair deal if you need gloves anyway.

A fit for a new composter who wants the tools in one box. The caveat is that the listing is unbranded, so check seller reviews and the return policy before you buy.
products.idealFor: New composters who want gloves in the same order.
products.skipIf: You prefer a documented brand over a bundle.

products.name: Compost Tumbler Bin Composter Dual Chamber 43 Gallon (Bundled with Pearson's Gardening Gloves), Alternate Listing
products.verdict: A second listing of the 43 gallon dual-chamber bundle with Pearson's gloves.
products.description:
This is a second listing for a 43 gallon dual-chamber tumbler bundled with Pearson's gardening gloves, in the same $50 to $100 bracket. Its photos differ from the first bundle, which may mean a different colour or finish.

It ranks seventh because it offers nothing the first bundle lacks, and the listing is just as short on detail. Choose between the two by which has the better delivery, price or finish on the day. Both trail the VIVOSUN and Werph because those are easier to research.

Buy it only if the first bundle is out of stock. The caveat is the same: unbranded, thinly documented, so confirm the frame and door details before you commit to a drum that you will be turning for years.
products.idealFor: Buyers who need the bundle when the first is out of stock.
products.skipIf: You want a documented brand or a steel frame.

products.name: FCMP Outdoor IM2000 Tumbling Composter Canadian-Made, 100% Recycled Resin
products.verdict: A 22 gallon Canadian-made tumbler in 100% recycled resin, sized for small yards.
products.description:
The FCMP IM2000 holds 22 gallons, is made in Canada and uses 100% recycled resin. It is the smallest drum in the ranking, in the $50 to $100 bracket, and the one most likely to fit on a balcony or a narrow side yard.

It ranks last because capacity is the limit. 22 gallons is about half the 43 gallon units and well under the Maygrove, so a busy household will fill it fast. Within that limit it has a clear appeal: recycled resin, a known maker and a footprint that suits small spaces.

Choose it for a one or two person household. The caveat is that a small drum fills quickly, so expect to wait out each batch before adding more.
products.idealFor: One or two person households with a small yard.
products.skipIf: You produce a lot of kitchen or garden waste.

methodology.title: Capacity
methodology.description: Stated drum size in gallons, because it sets how much waste you can process before a batch has to rest.

methodology.title: Chamber design
methodology.description: Whether the drum has dual chambers so one batch can mature while the other fills.

methodology.title: Frame and material
methodology.description: Steel, resin or unstated, since the stand carries the full weight of a loaded drum.

methodology.title: Doors and access
methodology.description: Door type and how well it keeps scraps in while giving you room to load and unload.

methodology.title: Value and documentation
methodology.description: Price bracket against how much the listing actually tells you about the product.

whatMatters.detail: A dual-chamber drum has a divider so you can fill one side while the other matures. Without it, you must stop adding scraps while a batch finishes. Look for the words dual chamber or batch in the title. For a household that produces scraps daily, two chambers matter more than extra gallons.

A full drum is heavy, and each turn puts that weight on the axle and stand. A weak frame flexes or cracks over time. Listings that mention solid steel, as Maygrove's does, tell you something; those that say nothing leave you guessing. Check the photos for how the drum attaches to the stand.

A bigger drum holds more waste but is heavier to turn when full, and compost needs air to work, so do not pack it to the brim. A 40 to 50 gallon unit suits most families; 22 gallons suits a small household. Check the gallon figure, and leave a third of the drum empty.

Doors let you add scraps and remove finished compost. Sliding doors resist spills; hinged lids can leak when the drum turns. A bad seal also lets in pests. Look for the door type in the title or photos, and check whether the door latches shut firmly.

Resin drums are light and rust-free, while steel is tougher but heavier. A black drum warms in sun, which speeds composting in cool climates. Choose a spot with partial sun and good drainage, and check whether the material suits your weather.

faq.q: Where should I put a compost tumbler?
faq.a: Choose a level spot with partial sun and room to rotate the drum. Heat helps composting, so a sunny corner suits a black drum like the Werph. Keep it near the kitchen or garden so you actually use it, and away from walls.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with tumblers?
faq.a: Overfilling the drum or loading only kitchen scraps. Compost needs browns such as leaves and cardboard as well as greens, and air to move through. Leave a third of the Maygrove or VIVOSUN empty so the mix can tumble.

faq.q: Is a dual-chamber tumbler worth it over a single drum?
faq.a: Yes, for steady waste. The Cozurra and Maygrove let one side cure while the other fills, so you never stop adding scraps. A single drum such as the FCMP IM2000 makes you pause while a batch finishes.

Assemble the stand, add a mix of green scraps and brown material, and give the drum a few turns every few days. Keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge. A new Maygrove or VIVOSUN needs the same routine.

faq.q: How do I maintain a compost tumbler?
faq.a: Check the frame bolts now and then, clear the door seal and keep the vents free. If compost smells sour, add dry browns and turn more often. On the FCMP steel drum, wipe off any residue before the winter.
Decomposition slows in the cold, but a black drum in sun stays warmer. The FCMP IM2000 and others keep working at a lower pace. Keep adding scraps and wait for spring to empty the finished batch.

finalTake: The Maygrove 53 gallon is the compost tumbler to buy if you want the most room and a stated steel frame, with the Cozurra a sensible step down. On a tighter budget, the VIVOSUN gives you two chambers for $50 to $100. Small yards should look at the FCMP IM2000. Fill the drum only two thirds full, turn it often and it will give you usable compost season after season.
